doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Art, reputations and being a professional writer
summary: Prompted by a line from his Ellington book, he talks about art not needing to be good, and why he is a professional writer, not an author.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Here’s a statement I thought was interesting. You said it was “one of the curiosities of twentieth century America that art does not have to be very good to establish its creator as a person of distinction. It’s only necessary that it be art.”
Well that’s true, where did I say that?
I believe in the Ellington book.

The Ellington book? Yeah it’s true. I mean it’s certainly true and I’m not going to start naming names, I’m in enough trouble as it is. But you have novelists who nobody wants to read and yet they do because they feel they must or at least they read enough of it to be able to talk about the book. But they have a literary reputation. And once you get that literary reputation on one book then you go along and you get asked to contribute to seminars or people call to ask your opinion on things or on whatever you’re doing. But do you have any readers? And I’m not saying that you’re supposed to go out and whore for the greatest amount of readers you can get, no. But I do feel that you should be talking to somebody. You’re not creating an artifact. You’re not making a rocking chair or selling a quilt. You’re not creating something. This is a system of communication. You’re telling somebody something. You’re talking to somebody. And if there’s nobody out on the other end listening I don’t quite see what the function of the thing is. Fine if you want

to do it, and sit home and do it and write because you like writing, that’s fine. But you know, these reputations very often, literary or artistic reputations come and go pretty fast. So I think that that’s true. And I do not like to call myself an author, I’m not an author, I’m a professional writer. That’s what I am. And the term, to say you’re a professional writer is almost pejorative because it means you might be concerned about story, it means you might be plotting, and so forth. It might be putting something in there that somebody might want to read. But that is what I am. I’m not an artist, I’m not an author. I’m a professional writer. And I happen to be a good one. But that’s the attitude I take toward this. And once you start getting literary you’re in trouble, you’re in trouble.
